newsitem.title: USA: Soft red winter wheat crops seen average to good.
newsitem.headline: Soft red winter wheat crops seen average to good.

text.p: The ongoing late harvest of the soybean crop in the eastern corn belt has left the soft red winter wheat crop in mostly average condition at this stage in the growing season, agronomists and crop specialists said.
"At this point I would characterize the crop as average," said Howard Siegrist, an extension agent in central Ohio for Ohio State University.
Siegrist said the lateness of the Ohio crop meant that most of the winter wheat crop is still in the ground and needed a week or two of warmer weather to jumpstart the crop's development.
"The crop is very late, and a lot of it is just now emerging," Siegrist said.
The Ohio Agricultural Statistics Service reported Tuesday that 78 percent of the winter wheat crop had emerged, compared to 93 percent last year and the five-year average of 89 percent.
The winter wheat crops in Illinois and Indiana are also behind, but agronomists there said that those crops looked better than last year's crops.
"From what I've seen in general, the crop looks pretty good," said Emerson Nafziger, agronomist with the University of Illinois in Champaign.
However, because wheat planting was also late in Illinois, the crop is registering less growth than it normally should and is not in optimal condition, Nafziger said.

According to the latest crop report from the Illinois Agricultural statistics service, the winter wheat crop was rated 17 percent excellent and 60 percent good during the week ended Sunday. Those ratings compared with an excellent rating 23 percent and a good rating of 54 percent the previous week
Because the eastern corn belt's soybean crop has still not been fully harvested in some areas, most agronomists expect to see a decline in acreage seeded to wheat.
In some parts of southern Indiana, wheat acreage could be down as much as 50 percent, and Siegris estimated total acreage in Ohio would be down five percent from average levels.

This week's cold snap across the Midwest was also seen hindering development of the crop. Several days of freezing temperatures could have arrested development in crops in some of the more nothern areas, agronomists said.
